summary: Collects general architectural and policy questions that the IETF community should consider when working on new standards and protocols. It is explicitly a list of questions to be addressed rather than guidelines or principles to follow.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building something new, it helps to ask good questions. This note is a checklist of big questions the Internet's rule writers should think about.

questions: internet policy questions for new protocols
subtitle: A checklist of architectural questions for IETF protocol designers.

tldr.problem: As the Internet architecture grew more complex, individual protocol designers focused narrowly on their layer of the protocol stack without considering how their work fit into the larger architectural picture, risking incoherent overall design.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a set of architectural and policy questions organized into categories—design justification, layering, long-term costs, robustness, deployment, and others—that working groups should consider when designing new protocols. It provides examples and case studies showing how real protocols have addressed (or failed to address) these questions.
tldr.outcome: The document serves as a guide for IETF members to evaluate and improve the architectural quality of new protocols and to promote coherence across the Internet architecture.

today: RFC 3426 remains a living architectural document. It is not standards-track; it serves as guidance for working groups evaluating new protocol proposals. The questions and case studies remain relevant as the IETF continues to grapple with protocol design trade-offs, especially as new issues (deployment on mobile networks, energy efficiency, security at scale) emerge.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
The RFC was motivated by concerns that the Internet architecture was losing coherence. The early Internet was designed by a small group with a unified vision. Today, development is distributed across many working groups, each with its own interests and expertise. This distribution is necessary, but it risks creating a patchwork of solutions optimized locally without considering global implications.

Unlike RFC 1958 (Architectural Principles of the Internet), which states guidelines to follow, this document poses questions to be addressed. The questions are not a checklist that every protocol must answer in detail—different protocols face different concerns—but a toolkit for working groups to think more comprehensively about their work.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet grew up and got more complicated. This RFC is a reminder to ask good questions before building something new.

sections.title: Core Design Questions
sections.content:
The first group of questions focuses on the design itself. Justification: Why propose this solution instead of an existing one or a different approach? The RFC uses integrated and differentiated services as examples: designers had to justify why new QoS architectures were needed and why they were better than alternatives.

Layering: At which layer of the protocol stack should this function sit? The RFC discusses the end-to-end argument, which suggests that low-level implementations of functions like reliability can be redundant if the application layer must verify them anyway. Sometimes the most obvious layer is not the best. The RFC cites examples of protocols layered on HTTP—convenient for traversing firewalls and reusing libraries, but adding overhead. Designers must weigh benefits against costs.

Long-term vs. short-term solutions: If this is not the best long-term solution, what are the costs of living with it temporarily? The RFC flags NAT traversal mechanisms as example short-term fixes: they work around a problem (NATs modifying addresses) without solving the underlying issue (why NATs exist in the first place). Any temporary solution should include an exit strategy and clear identification of problems it leaves unsolved.

The whole picture: Modern protocols often rely on pieces standardized in other working groups or bodies. SIP, for example, depends on SDP (from MMUSIC), extensions from SIPPING, and integration with call processing languages defined elsewhere. Designers must keep the larger context in mind while focusing on their specific piece.
sections.plainLanguage: Before designing, ask: Is this the right answer? Should it go here? Is this forever or temporary? And what else needs to happen for this to work?

sections.title: Questions for Evaluating Protocols
sections.content:
Benefits vs. costs: How do the architectural benefits compare to the costs? The RFC examines performance-enhancing proxies (PEPs) that optimize links but disable end-to-end security and add single points of failure. The costs are real and must be carefully weighed.

Robustness: How well does the protocol handle not just node failures but also buggy implementations, packet corruption, reordering, and malicious components? Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) illustrates this: the original design did not account for firewalls that drop or reset ECN-marked packets, a real-world problem the RFC had to address retroactively with workarounds.

Tragedy of the commons: Does performance remain robust if everyone uses this protocol? A transport protocol that assumes it is the only traffic-shaping mechanism might perform well individually but cause congestion collapse if widely adopted without end-to-end congestion control.

Competing interests: Does the protocol protect all stakeholders—end users, ISPs, equipment vendors, software vendors? Or does it privilege one party at another's expense? Using codepoints in IP headers for QoS, rather than binding QoS to port numbers, is cited as good design because it allows room for different business models to coexist.

Choice vs. complexity: Is the protocol designed to let different players express preferences where appropriate, or is it overloaded with options that threaten interoperability? SIP has faced this tension: it is designed for extensibility, but excessive options risk inconsistent implementations.

Evolvability: Does the protocol preserve the Internet's ability to evolve? Does it make unreasonable assumptions about the network that could constrain future development? The RFC warns against overloading existing protocols (like DNS) with too much new functionality, and against failures of transparency (firewalls, middleboxes) that make it harder for new technologies to emerge.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask: Is this fair to everyone? Will it still work when things go wrong? Will it still work at scale? Does it leave room for the future to change?

sections.title: Other Important Considerations
sections.content:
Internationalization: If the protocol uses text, have the conflicting needs of global comprehensibility and local language support been addressed? DNS faces this tension: domain names should be universally decodable (currently, case-independent ASCII), but users expect to see them in their local scripts. This is a complex problem the RFC notes but does not solve.

Deployability: Can this protocol actually be deployed in the real Internet? Designers often overlook deployment difficulties. The RFC notes that QoS architectures faced deployment barriers (administrative boundaries, lack of incentives), IPv6 deployment has been slow (due to transition complexity and lack of perceived urgency), and Integrated Services deployment was limited by assumptions about how the network is managed.

A protocol is more deployable if it works in a realistic Internet: it must handle dropped, reordered, duplicated, and rerouted packets; work with pre-existing standards; and function in the presence of middleboxes and asymmetric routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Can people around the world use this? Will it work with the messy Internet that actually exists?

sections.title: How to Use This Document
sections.content:
The RFC is not intended as a rigid checklist. Some questions apply more to one protocol than another. A simple, single-purpose protocol may not need to address all topics deeply. The document's value lies in prompting comprehensive thinking: have we considered this aspect, and if we decided to ignore it, did we do so deliberately?

The case studies (integrated services, SIP, ECN, OPES, performance-enhancing proxies) show how real protocols have wrestled with these questions. They illustrate both good decision-making and cautionary tales. The RFC encourages others to contribute case studies, especially for controversial decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a thinking tool, not a rule book. Use it to make sure you have thought about the big picture before you lock in your design.

items.title: Justification
items.text: Why this solution instead of existing alternatives?

items.title: Layering
items.text: Which protocol layer is the right place for this function?

items.title: Long-term viability
items.text: Is this a permanent fix or a temporary workaround with known costs?

items.title: System integration
items.text: How does this fit with other protocols and standards bodies' work?

items.title: Robustness
items.text: How well does this handle failures, bugs, and malicious behavior?

items.title: Scalability
items.text: Does it still work well if everyone uses it at the same time?

items.title: Fairness
items.text: Does it balance the interests of all stakeholders?

items.title: Future-proofing
items.text: Does it leave room for the Internet architecture to evolve?
